title: Transaction Isolation Levels
description: Explore SQL Server's isolation levels, from READ UNCOMMITTED to SERIALIZABLE, and learn how each level trades consistency, concurrency, and blocking.

data.text: Transaction isolation levels are SQL Server's way of letting you control the trade-off between **data consistency** and **concurrency**. At one extreme, a system that allows only one transaction at a time is perfectly consistent but useless in production. At the other extreme, a system that lets everyone read and write simultaneously is fast but dangerous. Isolation levels let you pick the right balance for each workload.

SQL Server supports five isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, SNAPSHOT, and SERIALIZABLE. Each level prevents different anomalies — dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads — and each imposes different locking behavior.
Before diving into isolation levels, it helps to understand the problems they solve. The three classic concurrency anomalies are:

data.title: Concurrency Anomalies
items: Dirty Read — a transaction reads data that another transaction has modified but not yet committed, which may later be rolled back
Non-repeatable Read — a transaction reads the same row twice and gets different values because another transaction modified and committed it between the reads
Phantom Read — a transaction re-executes a query returning rows that satisfy a condition and sees new rows that were inserted by another committed transaction

rows: No shared locks; uses NOLOCK behavior
Shared locks held only during read; released immediately after
Shared locks held until transaction ends
No shared locks; uses row versioning from tempdb
Range locks (key-range locks) held until transaction ends

data.text: You can set the isolation level at the session level with `SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL`, or you can use table hints on individual queries. Session-level settings apply to every query in that connection until changed or the connection closes.

data.title: Setting Isolation Levels in T-SQL
data.content: Examples of setting different isolation levels and using table hints.

data.title: READ COMMITTED Is the Default for a Reason
data.text: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads while keeping blocking manageable. It is the right choice for the vast majority of OLTP workloads. Only move to higher isolation levels when you have a specific consistency requirement that READ COMMITTED cannot satisfy.

Choosing an isolation level is not about picking the 'safest' option. It is about understanding the consistency requirements of your workload and matching them to the locking and blocking behavior you can tolerate. Over-isolating a high-concurrency OLTP system is just as harmful as under-isolating a financial ledger.

data.title: Guidelines for Isolation Level Selection
items: READ COMMITTED — default for most OLTP; prevents dirty reads with minimal blocking
READ UNCOMMITTED — only for approximate reporting where dirty reads are acceptable
REPEATABLE READ — use when a transaction must read the same data multiple times without changes
SNAPSHOT — ideal for high-concurrency reporting and BI workloads; eliminates most reader-writer blocking
SERIALIZABLE — use only for critical consistency scenarios where phantoms are unacceptable; it has the highest blocking cost

data.title: Snapshot Requires Tempdb
data.text: SNAPSHOT and READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT isolation store row versions in tempdb. If tempdb is undersized or slow, these isolation levels can become a performance bottleneck rather than a benefit.

items.question: Can I change the isolation level mid-transaction?
items.answer: No. The isolation level is set at the beginning of a transaction and cannot be changed until the transaction ends. You must commit or roll back before switching.

items.question: Does READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT change the default isolation level?
items.answer: No. READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT (RCSI) changes the behavior of the existing READ COMMITTED level to use row versioning instead of shared locks. It does not change the isolation level itself — queries still run under READ COMMITTED, but they no longer acquire shared locks for reads.

items.question: What is the performance impact of SNAPSHOT isolation?
items.answer: SNAPSHOT reduces blocking significantly for read-heavy workloads, but it increases tempdb I/O because every row modification generates a version copy. In write-heavy systems with frequent updates to the same rows, tempdb can become a bottleneck.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Isolation levels control the trade-off between consistency and concurrency in SQL Server
READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads with minimal blocking — it is the right default for most production systems
SNAPSHOT and RCSI eliminate most reader-writer blocking by using row versioning, but they increase tempdb usage
SERIALIZABLE provides the strongest guarantees but can cause severe blocking; use it only when phantoms are unacceptable
You cannot change isolation level mid-transaction — plan your transaction boundaries accordingly
data.takeaway: Isolation levels are not about choosing the 'most safe' setting; they are about aligning data consistency guarantees with your workload's blocking tolerance.
